roles.title: GRC Analyst
roles.subtitle: Entry to Mid-level | Governance, Risk & Compliance

questions.q: Walk me through how you would conduct a risk assessment for a new SaaS vendor.
questions.a: I would start with the vendor's criticality classification is it processing PII, PHI, or financial data? Then I would map to our risk framework (NIST CSF or ISO 27001). Key steps: 1) Send SIG Lite or CAIQ questionnaire, 2) Review SOC 2 Type II (look for complementary user entity controls), 3) Check sub-processor list and flow-down clauses, 4) Assess data residency and cross-border transfer mechanisms (SCCs, adequacy), 5) Score inherent vs residual risk, 6) Document in risk register with treatment plan and owner. Red flags: no SOC 2, no DPA, sub-processors without flow-downs.

questions.q: How do you map controls across ISO 27001, SOC 2, and NIST CSF without duplicating work?
questions.a: I use a unified control framework typically NIST CSF as the backbone since it is outcome-based. Build a control catalog where each control has mappings: ISO 27001 Annex A control to SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria to NIST CSF subcategory. Example: Encryption at rest maps to A.10.1, CC6.7, PR.DS-1. Maintain in a tool like Drata or Vanta or a structured spreadsheet. When evidence is collected (config screenshot, policy doc), tag it once and it satisfies all three. Saves 60-70 percent effort vs. siloed approach.

questions.q: A critical control failed its test during internal audit. What is your process?
questions.a: First, classify the finding is it a design deficiency (control missing) or operating effectiveness (control exists but failed)? Immediate steps: 1) Notify control owner and stakeholder within 24h, 2) Root cause analysis (5 Whys), 3) Assess compensating controls do we have detective controls that caught it? 4) Remediation plan with owner, deadline, and evidence of fix, 5) Retest before next audit cycle. If it is a key control for SOC 2 or ISO, escalate to management immediately may need to disclose in management representation letter. Document everything in audit management tool.

roles.title: Privacy Engineer
roles.subtitle: Mid to Senior | Data Protection and Privacy by Design

questions.q: How do you implement Privacy by Design for a new AI feature that uses customer data for model training?
questions.a: Start at design phase not after. Steps: 1) DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) per GDPR Art⁄35 assess necessity, proportionality, risks to rights. 2) Data minimization can we use synthetic data or anonymized subsets? 3) Purpose limitation explicit consent or legitimate interest assessment (LIA) documented. 3) Technical controls: differential privacy (epsilon budget), federated learning if possible, output filtering for PII regurgitation. 4) Data subject rights pipeline: automated deletion from training sets (right to be forgotten), access request API. 5) Model cards documenting data sources, retention, deletion process. 6) DPA with ML platform vendor if using third-party. Document everything for supervisory authority.

questions.q: How do you handle a Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) when data spans 15-plus systems including data lakes and ML models?
questions.a: Automation is non-negotiable. Build a DSAR orchestration layer: 1) Identity verification workflow (2FA plus doc check). 2) Data discovery maintain a data catalog (Atlan or Amundsen) with PII tags per table/column. 3) Orchestration engine queries each system via API (Snowflake, S3, Kafka, PostgreSQL, ML feature store). 4) ML model challenge extract training data influence (SHAP values, influence functions) or retrain without subject data if required. 5) Deduplication and review UI for privacy team. 5) Deliver in machine-readable format (JSON or CSV) within 30 days (GDPR) or 45 days (CCPA). Track SLA in Jira. Test quarterly with synthetic requests.

questions.q: Explain the difference between anonymization and pseudonymization under GDPR, and when you would use each.
questions.a: Pseudonymization (Art⁄4(5)) replace identifiers with tokens or keys, re-identification possible with additional info. Still personal data under GDPR. Use when you need re-identification (e.g., clinical trials, fraud detection). Anonymization irreversible, no reasonable likelihood of re-identification. Falls outside GDPR scope. Use for analytics, ML training, public datasets. Key test: reasonable likelihood considering cost, time, technology. Techniques: k-anonymity (k=5 or more), l-diversity, t-closeness, differential privacy (epsilon less than 1). Never claim anonymization if you hold the re-identification key.

roles.title: Security Engineer
roles.subtitle: Mid to Senior | Cloud Security, AppSec, Detection

questions.q: How do you secure CI/CD pipelines for a microservices architecture?
questions.a: Defense in depth across the pipeline: 1) Source: Branch protection (required reviews, signed commits, SAST⁄SCA on every PR Semgrep, CodeQL, Trivy). 2) Build: Immutable base images (Distroless), SBOM generation (Syft), image signing (Cosign⁄Notary), vulnerability scanning with fail thresholds (Critical⁄High = fail). 3) Registry: Admission controller (Kyverno⁄OPA) enforces signed images, no latest tags, resource limits. 4) Deploy: GitOps (ArgoCD⁄Flux) with drift detection, canary⁄blue-green deployments. 5) Runtime: Falco⁄Sysdig for runtime threat detection, network policies (Cilium), Pod Security Standards. 6) Secrets: Vault⁄SealedSecrets, no secrets in Git. Rotate keys quarterly.

questions.q: How do you detect and respond to a potential cloud credential leak in a public repo?
questions.a: Speed is everything. Automated response: 1) Push protection GitHub⁄GitLab secret scanning plus TruffleHog⁄TruffleHog Enterprise on every push (block if secret detected). 2) If leaked: immediate revocation via cloud provider API (AWS IAM, GCP IAM, Azure AD). 3) Rotate all potentially exposed keys enumerate via cloud asset inventory. 4) CloudTrail⁄Cloud Audit Logs review for anomalous API calls (geo-impossible, unusual services, privilege escalation). 5) Incident ticket with timeline, blast radius assessment, customer notification if required (GDPR 72h, SEC 4-day). 6) Post-incident: secret scanning in CI, secret rotation automation, developer training. Tooling: GitGuardian, TruffleHog, AWS Macie, GCP Secret Manager.

questions.q: How do you implement zero-trust network architecture in a hybrid cloud environment?
questions.a: Never trust, always verify. Pillars: 1) Identity: IdP (Okta⁄Entra ID) plus MFA plus conditional access (device compliance, location, risk score). 2) Device: MDM (Jamf⁄Intune) plus device trust scores, certificate-based auth. 3) Network: Micro-segmentation (Cilium⁄Calico in K8s, AWS Security Groups or Azure NSG or GCP Firewall), no implicit trust zones. 4) Application: mTLS everywhere (Istio⁄Linkerd), JWT validation at gateway (Envoy⁄Kong), short-lived certs (SPIFFE⁄SPIRE). 4) Data: Encryption in transit (TLS 1.3), at rest (KMS), DLP at egress. 6) Visibility: Zero-trust network access (ZTNA) replacing VPN, continuous verification. Tools: Tailscale⁄NetBird for mesh, Cloudflare Access, BeyondCorp principles.

roles.title: CISO / Security Leader
roles.subtitle: Senior Leadership | Strategy, Board Communication, Culture

questions.q: How do you communicate cyber risk to the Board in business terms?
questions.a: Translate technical risk to business impact. Framework: 1) Risk quantification use FAIR model (Frequency times Loss Magnitude) to express in dollars (e.g., Ransomware: 15% annual likelihood, $2.3M expected loss). 2) Heat map with business objectives (revenue, reputation, regulatory, operations). 2) Show trend risk posture improving/degrading? 3) Investment asks tied to risk reduction: Investing $500k in EDR reduces ransomware risk by 40% = $920K risk reduction. 4) Regulatory landscape updates (SEC 4-day disclosure, NIS2, DORA). 5) Peer benchmarking. Keep it to 3 slides max. No jargon. Own the narrative.

questions.q: How do you build a security culture where developers own security?
questions.a: Shift from gatekeeper to enabler. 1) Embed security in DevEx paved roads (secure defaults, golden paths), not gates. 2) Security Champions program 1 champion per 8-10 devs, 20% time allocation, direct line to AppSec. 3) Gamify capture-the-flag, bug bounty internal, leaderboards. 4) Blameless postmortems focus on systemic fixes, not individuals. 5) Metrics developers care about: deploy frequency, MTTR, change failure rate (DORA). 5) Executive sponsorship CISO presents at all-hands, celebrates security wins. Budget for developer security training (not compliance checkbox). Make secure the easy path.

questions.q: You discover a critical vulnerability in a core product on Friday 5pm. Walk me through your decision process.
questions.a: Speed with discipline. 1) Assemble tiger team (Security, Engineering, Product, Legal, Comms) within 30 min. 2) Assess: exploitability (public exploit? active exploitation?), blast radius (customers affected, data at risk), patch complexity. 3) Decision matrix: if CVSS 9.0+ plus active exploit plus customer data at risk emergency patch within 24h regardless of day. 4) Coordinate with Legal on disclosure obligations (coordinated vulnerability disclosure, CVE request). 5) Customer communication: transparent, actionable (workarounds, patch timeline), no marketing spin. 6) Post-incident: root cause, SDLC gap analysis, prevent recurrence. Document decision rationale for regulators. Sleep when it is patched.

roles.title: Compliance Manager
roles.subtitle: Mid-level | Audit Management, Evidence, Regulatory Tracking

questions.q: How do you manage evidence collection for SOC 2 Type II across 50-plus controls without burning out your team?
questions.a: Automate 80%, human-review 20%. 1) Continuous control monitoring (CCM) integrate with AWS Config, GitHub, Okta, Jira, PagerDuty to auto-collect evidence (config snapshots, PR approvals, access reviews, incident timestamps). 2) Control ownership matrix each control has a named owner (not security team), SLA for evidence upload. 3) Continuous monitoring dashboard red/yellow/green per control, automated reminders 30⁄15⁄7 days before due. 4) Sampling strategy for high-volume controls (e.g., access reviews), test 25% quarterly, rotate sample. 5) Auditor collaboration pre-audit walkthrough, agree on evidence format early. Tooling: Drata⁄Vanta⁄Thoropass for automation, Notion⁄Confluence for narrative. Goal: audit becomes non-event.

questions.q: How do you track regulatory changes across 15-plus jurisdictions and assess impact?
questions.a: Structured horizon scanning. 1) Sources: RegTech feeds (OneTrust, Metricstream, LexisNexis), regulator RSS (EDPB, ICO, CPPA, FTC), law firm alerts, industry ISACs. 2) Triage: regulatory change to classification (new law, amendment, guidance, enforcement) to applicability assessment (do we operate there? process that data?) to impact rating (High⁄Med⁄Low) to action owner plus deadline. 3) Dashboard: regulation, effective date, status (monitoring⁄implementing⁄compliant), evidence of compliance. 4) Quarterly regulatory update to leadership. 5) Legal partnership quarterly sync with outside counsel. Tooling: OneTrust⁄Metricstream for regulatory change management, Notion for tracking.
